extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners who practice before the USPTO (particularly trademark attorneys) and Office of Enrollment and Discipline staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures governing discipline of practitioners before the United States Patent and Trademark Office, including definitions of practitioner status, prohibited conduct (unauthorized practice), supervisory responsibilities, settlement/processing under 37 C.F.R. §11.26, and prescribed sanctions and publication requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner status and authority to practice before the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney licensed and in good standing to practice law in a U.S. state is authorized under 5 U.S.C. § 500(b) to practice before the USPTO; such an attorney is a 'practitioner' as defined by 37 C.F.R. § 10.1(r)(2) and is subject to the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility set forth at 37 C.F.R. § 10.20 et seq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being a state-licensed attorney (and thus a 'practitioner' under 37 C.F.R. §10.1(r)(2)) brings an individual within the disciplinary rules of the USPTO; practitioners are bound by 37 C.F.R. § 10.20(b) and related provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO jurisdiction over disciplinary matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over disciplinary matters pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.20(a)(3) and 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary proceedings and approval of settlement agreements are processed under these statutory and regulatory provisions; the OED Director and USPTO Director exercise authority under them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on delegating signature/authority to non-lawyers
rubrics_metrics.description: Under USPTO rules of practice, an attorney may not delegate authority for a non-lawyer to sign documents to be filed with the Office. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP § 611.01(b) specifically states that an authorized signatory must personally sign his/her name and another person (paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of an attorney. Allowing a non-attorney to sign filings violates USPTO rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized practice of law prohibition (aiding unauthorized practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who aids another in the unauthorized practice of law before the Office violates 37 C.F.R. § 10.47; negligently allowing a non-attorney to practice trademark law before the USPTO constitutes such a violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example factual posture: a non-attorney prepared, signed and filed a trademark application and responses to Office actions; the attorney who knew or should have known about these acts is subject to discipline under § 10.47.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility to supervise non-attorney contractors and employees
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner engages or contracts with a non-attorney (e.g., corporation service company employee) to assist in filing and prosecuting matters before the USPTO, the practitioner remains responsible for overseeing that individual's work and ensuring compliance with USPTO rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Client consent to hiring a third party does not relieve the practitioner of responsibility; permitting a non-attorney to sign or otherwise practice before the Office is negligent and can lead to disciplinary sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement agreement requirements under 37 C.F.R. § 11.26
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proposed Settlement Agreement resolving disciplinary complaints must satisfy the requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 11.26; such an agreement sets forth stipulated facts, legal conclusions, and agreed sanctions to resolve disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Proposed Settlement Agreement meets § 11.26 requirements, it may be submitted to the USPTO Director (or designate) for approval and can resolve all disciplinary action arising from the stipulated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and remedial actions for violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary sanctions can include a public reprimand, publication of the Final Order, publication of a Notice in the Official Gazette, notice of public discipline to state disciplinary agencies and courts, and allocation of costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order in this matter ordered: (a) public reprimand of the respondent; (b) OED Director shall publish the Final Order; (c) OED Director shall publish a Notice in the Official Gazette; (d) OED Director shall notify disciplinary enforcement agencies in the practitioner's admitting state and courts where admitted; (e) the parties shall each bear their own costs incurred to date and in carrying out the terms of the agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and public accessibility of disciplinary decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary decisions involving practitioners are to be posted at the Office of Enrollment and Discipline's Reading Room and may be summarized in the Official Gazette (e.g., Notice of Reprimand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order includes an explicit Notice of Reprimand text and references the OED Reading Room URL (http://des.uspto.gov/Foia/OEDReadingRoom.jsp) as the public posting location for disciplinary decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between trademark practice and patent practitioner registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorization to practice trademark law before the USPTO (e.g., as a state-licensed attorney) does not equate to being a registered patent practitioner; a respondent authorized to practice trademark law was explicitly noted as 'not a registered patent practitioner and is not authorized to practice patent law before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public notices may explicitly state the scope of a practitioner's authorization (trademark vs. patent practice) to avoid confusion about practitioner credentials and permitted practice areas before the Office.
